title: Joins: pairing rows across tables
explanation:
A **join** combines rows from two tables, with an `ON` condition saying which rows belong together. Conceptually the database considers every pairing and keeps those where `ON` is true. So the result has one row **per matching pair**: a customer with three orders appears three times. That repetition is the join's *grain* — know it before you count or sum anything.

```sql
SELECT o.order_id, c.name
FROM orders AS o
JOIN customers AS c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id;
```

An **inner join** (`JOIN`) drops rows that have no match. A **`LEFT JOIN`** keeps every row of the left table at least once; when there is no match, the right table's columns are filled with `NULL`. That makes "who has no orders?" a `LEFT JOIN ... WHERE o.order_id IS NULL`.

Where you put a condition matters with `LEFT JOIN`: a condition in `ON` only limits which right-hand rows match, while the same condition in `WHERE` filters the final rows — and it throws away the `NULL`-filled rows you meant to keep.
keyIdeas: A join yields one row per matching pair — check the grain.
`LEFT JOIN` keeps every left row; missing right columns become `NULL`.
Right-table filters belong in `ON` when you must keep unmatched left rows.

workedExample.problem: Data: customers above; products `(1,'Green tea','tea',8)`, `(2,'Black tea','tea',12)`, `(3,'Oolong','tea',15)`, `(4,'Teapot','ware',30)`, `(5,'Cup','ware',6)`; orders `(10,1,…,'paid')`, `(11,1,…,'paid')`, `(12,2,…,'cancelled')`, `(13,3,…,'paid')`, `(14,2,…,'paid')`, `(15,4,…,'pending')`; order_items `(1,10,1,2)`, `(2,10,5,2)`, `(3,11,4,1)`, `(4,12,2,3)`, `(5,13,3,1)`, `(6,13,1,4)`, `(7,14,2,2)`, `(8,15,5,1)`. For **paid** orders, list each tea item's customer city, product name, and quantity.
steps: Needed columns span four tables: city (customers), status (orders), quantity (order_items), name and category (products).
Chain the joins along the keys: customers → orders on `customer_id`, orders → order_items on `order_id`, order_items → products on `product_id`.
The grain is one row per order item, so a product bought twice appears twice.
Filter with `WHERE o.status = 'paid' AND p.category = 'tea'`, then sort for a stable result.

Run it:
```sql
SELECT c.city, p.name, oi.quantity
FROM customers AS c
JOIN orders AS o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
JOIN order_items AS oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
JOIN products AS p ON p.product_id = oi.product_id
WHERE o.status = 'paid' AND p.category = 'tea'
ORDER BY c.city, p.name, oi.quantity;
```
workedExample.answer:
4 rows:

| city | name | quantity |
|---|---|---|
| Lima | Green tea | 2 |
| Lima | Green tea | 4 |
| Lima | Oolong | 1 |
| Quito | Black tea | 2 |

pitfalls: Summing a column after joining to a many-row table, so each value is counted once per match.
Filtering the right table of a `LEFT JOIN` in `WHERE`, which silently turns it into an inner join.
Forgetting the `ON` condition (or joining on the wrong key), which pairs every row with every row.
